title: The Name Ceremony
philosophicalAnchor: The Namakarana does not create the child. The name is not the child. The name is a relationship between the child and the world. Names are not objects; names refer to objects; an object can have many names; renaming does not change the object.
pythonConcept: variables, references, id(), is vs ==, None, naming conventions, garbage collection, rebinding
briefDescription: Explore Python's object model through the Namakarana naming ceremony, understanding how names refer to objects.
theoryPillar: Python creates objects before binding names. x = 10 creates integer 10 first, then binds x to it. Objects exist independently of names. Multiple names can refer to the same object. del removes a name, not necessarily the object.
anchorPillar: Indian naming ceremonies follow rules, just as Python has naming conventions. The name given to a child is a label, not the child itself. Multiple relatives calling the same name all refer to the same child.
triggerPillar: At the naming ceremony, the child exists before being named. x = 10 creates the object before binding the name. a = b = [] makes both names refer to same list. Modifying through one name affects what both see.
realityPillar: type() reveals object class. id() returns memory address. is checks identity, == checks equality. Small integers are interned (reused). del removes name references. Garbage collector reclaims objects with no remaining references.
